راتب.etymology: From the Arabic root ر ت ب, associated with being fixed or established. The adjective راتب can describe something regular or enduring; as a noun it names an employee’s pay for a specified period.
راتب.notes: The Cairo Academy records both the wage sense and the expression for a fixed, regular livelihood. This is a documented semantic connection, not a proposed date for the first use of salary. The lesson uses the noun meaning salary.

history.meaning: fixed or regular; salary paid for work

sources.title: Cairo Arabic Language Academy: رتب, especially الراتب and المرتب

مصروف.etymology: An Arabic formation from ص ر ف, a family which includes spending money. The shape مفعول is the passive-participle pattern; the noun مصروف denotes money for expenses or an allowance.
مصروف.notes: The Academy explicitly records صرف المال for spending money. The passive-pattern analysis explains the formation, while the allowance sense in this lesson is established by the original Saudi dialogue. It is not a claim that every occurrence means pocket money.

morphemes.meaning: passive-participle formation; not a separate suffix

rootFamily.gloss: spend money; also turn or redirect
currency exchange; morphology, in other contexts

sources.title: Cairo Arabic Language Academy: صرف, especially spending money and المصرف

شهري.etymology: A relational adjective formed from شهر, month, with the Arabic adjective-forming ending ي. The feminine singular form adds ة: شهرية.
شهري.notes: The Academy explicitly identifies الشهري as belonging to or derived from الشهر and records الشهرية for a payment fixed by month. This is month → monthly morphology; it does not imply every word in the broader root family has a time-related meaning.

sources.title: Cairo Arabic Language Academy: شهر, especially الشهر, الشهري and الشهرية

مسؤول.etymology: An Arabic passive-participle formation from سأل, ask or call someone to account. The accountability sense connects being responsible with having to answer for a person or matter.
مسؤول.notes: The Academy groups the responsible person under سأل and describes a duty whose consequences fall on that person. In this lesson مسؤول is an adjective; the related noun can mean an official. That noun sense must not replace the contextual gloss responsible.

morphemes.meaning: passive-participle formation: one who is answerable

sources.title: Cairo Arabic Language Academy: سأل, especially المسؤول and المسؤولية

يعني.etymology: A lexicalised form of the Arabic verb عنى, meaning to intend or mean something by one’s words. Its verbal shape literally corresponds to “it means”, but in conversation it also serves as a marker for explanation, qualification or self-correction.
يعني.notes: Mobarki documents the marker’s varied narrative functions, and discourse research identifies its verbal lexical source. English I mean is a contextual translation here; the Arabic word retains the shape of a third-person verb.

sources.title: Cairo Arabic Language Academy: عنى, especially intending something by speech
Yahya Mobarki, Yaʕni as an Evaluative Discourse Marker, Arabic Linguistics Journal 15 (2022),250–276
Getting to the point: The discourse marker yaʕni in unplanned discourse in Cairene Arabic (2016)

قصد.etymology: An Arabic verbal noun in the ق ص د family. The verb قصد covers directing oneself deliberately toward a target and intending something by an utterance. The noun’s sense intention belongs to that same semantic family.
قصد.notes: The Academy records physical direction and intended meaning side by side in this family. In the source form قصدي, the final ي adds first-person possession: my intention, naturally what I mean in this context.

sources.title: Cairo Arabic Language Academy: قصد, especially قصد بقولِه and the noun القصد

احتاج.etymology: The Arabic form-VIII verb of the weak-root family ح و ج, need or lack. It shares that family with حاجة, a need, and محتاج, someone in need. The extra ت belongs to the derived verb pattern; it is not another root consonant.
احتاج.notes: The Academy lists احتاج beside حاج, need or lack. The root’s middle و is absent from the spelling of احتاج and يحتاج, where the stem contains a long vowel. In the source form يحتاجون, ي begins the third-person form and ون marks the plural subject.

morphemes.meaning: the form-VIII shape used by this lexical verb

sources.title: Cairo Arabic Language Academy: حاج, احتاج, الحاجة and محتاج in the أحوج definition

اسم.etymology: The Arabic noun name is also the traditional grammatical term for a noun. Its derivation was disputed within early Arabic grammar: the Basran analysis connected it with س م و, elevation, while the Kufan analysis connected it with و س م, marking.
اسم.notes: Olivieri documents the old dispute and concludes that morphology and Semitic cognates argue against the marking analysis. The semantic connection with elevation belongs to the traditional grammatical explanation. The Academy files اسم under سمو and records أسماء. In the source form اسمه, the ending adds his or its.

history.meaning: name; also the grammatical category noun

sources.title: Cairo Arabic Language Academy: الاسم and أسماء
Simona Olivieri, The ism in the Arabic Grammatical Tradition, JAIS 17, especially pp. 337–342

أنا.etymology: An inherited independent first-person pronoun. Al-Jallad reconstructs the short form *ʔanā for Proto-Arabic and records the consonantal spelling ʾn in Safaitic. The longer Semitic form *ʔanāku is not attested as an Arabic word in his comparison.
أنا.notes: The starred form is reconstructed, not a surviving inscription. Historical vowel lengths and their later changes are partly hypothetical; the entry does not prescribe one pronunciation for every modern dialect. The Academy identifies أنا as I for either a male or a female speaker.

history.meaning: independent I; vowels are not written in this form

sources.title: Ahmad Al-Jallad, A Manual of the Historical Grammar of Arabic, version 2019-1,§ 2.1, p. 47
Cairo Arabic Language Academy: أنا

عن.etymology: A long-established Arabic preposition with spatial and relational uses. The Academy records separation or passing beyond among its meanings, alongside substitution, cause and associated circumstances. It remains a complete function word, not a modern verb-derived abbreviation.
عن.notes: The responsibility relation appears in the classical quotation recorded in the Academy’s مسؤول entry, using مسؤول عن. This gives the lesson’s construction an older Arabic textual parallel. English for is the natural translation of the preposition in this particular relation.

history.stage: Classical Arabic construction recorded by the Academy
history.meaning: answerable for a person or matter

sources.title: Cairo Arabic Language Academy: عن
Cairo Arabic Language Academy: المسؤول and its quoted responsibility construction

كل.etymology: The Arabic quantifier for the whole of a group or all the parts of something, already used in classical texts cited by the Academy. Its established family includes كلما, whenever, which the Academy analyses as كل followed by ما in a general expression of time.
كل.notes: The quantifier corresponds to all, each or every according to the following expression. Here it includes the entire definite group of people. The related time expression كلما shows the same totality word combined with ما in the meaning whenever.

history.stage: Classical Arabic uses recorded by the Academy
history.meaning: all members or parts of the following expression

sources.title: Cairo Arabic Language Academy: كل, especially totality and the time expression with ما
Abdelkader Fassi Fehri, Hidden Trilogies of Universal Quantifiers (2020)

ناس.etymology: The collective people has competing traditional derivations. Lane records an analysis of ناس as a reduced form of أناس, associated with the human-being vocabulary, and another analysis connecting it with نوس, movement. The Academy files it under نوس and gives إنسان as its corresponding singular from a different word form.
ناس.notes: The competing derivations are attributed to lexicographers, whose explanations differ. In the lesson, الناس adds the definite article to the collective. Its corresponding singular إنسان has a different word form; the pair uses different stems.

sources.title: Cairo Arabic Language Academy: الناس
Edward William Lane, Arabic–English Lexicon: نوس, entry ناس and its competing derivations

اللي.etymology: An established spoken-Arabic relative marker belonging to the history of levelling the older relative-pronoun system. Galal contrasts the many gender, number and case forms of Classical and Standard Arabic with dialectal illi, which serves those functions with one invariant form.
اللي.notes: Galal’s review already reports illi as widespread in the comparative description of 1959, rather than dating its first appearance. His examples cover Egyptian, Moroccan, Syrian and Kuwaiti varieties. The Saudi lesson gives a local example of the invariant marker after the definite word for people.

history.stage: Comparative Arabic dialect descriptions reported by Galal
history.meaning: invariant relative marker who, which or that

sources.title: Mohamed Galal, Relativizer illi in Arabic Dialects (2004),especially pp. 44–46

برا.etymology: The spoken outside adverb continues Arabic spatial vocabulary recorded as بَرًّا in older lexicography, associated with بَرّ, open land or the exterior. Lane records phrases meaning sit outside the house and go outside a house or town under this entry.
برا.notes: Lane preserves al-Azhari’s judgement that those outside phrases were post-classical, reflecting an older debate about literary usage. The Academy records the related exterior adjective براني. In today’s lesson, برا means beyond the meeting room; the same location word can also refer to being outdoors.

history.stage: Earlier Arabic spatial usage recorded by Lane
history.meaning: outside a house or town; some lexicographers called these phrases post-classical

sources.title: Edward William Lane, Arabic–English Lexicon: بر,especially برّ signification B6
Cairo Arabic Language Academy: البر and البراني
